question: An 8-year-old boy presents to your office for a routine well-child visit. Upon physical examination, he is found to have a harsh-sounding, holosystolic murmur that is best appreciated at the left sternal border. The murmur becomes louder when you ask him to make fists with his hands. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Holosystolic murmur" -> "Best heard at left sternal border" -> "Murmur increases with handgrip" -> "Increased systemic vascular resistance" -> "Ventricular septal defect" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Holosystolic murmur" -> "Best heard at left sternal border" -> "Murmur increases with handgrip" -> "Increased afterload" -> "Ventricular septal defect" -> 90%
CHAIN: "Holosystolic murmur" -> "Best heard at left sternal border" -> "Murmur increases with handgrip" -> "Increased left-to-right shunt" -> "Ventricular septal defect" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Holosystolic murmur" -> "Best heard at left sternal border" -> "Murmur increases with handgrip" -> "Increased systemic vascular resistance" -> "Possible ventricular septal defect" -> 80%
analysis: The presence of a harsh-sounding, holosystolic murmur best heard at the left sternal border in a child is most commonly associated with a ventricular septal defect (VSD). The murmur becomes louder with increased systemic vascular resistance, such as when the child makes fists, which is consistent with a VSD. This maneuver increases afterload, causing more blood to shunt from left to right across the defect, thereby intensifying the murmur.
